planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun on well-drained, even poor sandy soil, with a male pollinator growing within 50-100 feet.

directions: Sirola is a female sea buckthorn selection noted for its upright, relatively narrow growth habit and comparatively few thorns compared with older wild-type selections, which makes hand harvest noticeably easier. It bears heavy clusters of large, sweet-tart orange berries on long stalks that hang somewhat clear of the foliage, another trait that speeds picking. Like all sea buckthorn it is dioecious and needs a male plant nearby for pollination, and its nitrogen-fixing roots let it thrive in lean, sandy, or coastal soils where little else fruits well. Established plants are extremely drought and wind tolerant and need almost no supplemental feeding once settled in.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, with a male sea buckthorn planted within 50-100 feet for pollination.

directions: Frugana is a vigorous, heavy-cropping female sea buckthorn valued as much for its ornamental show as for its harvest, with graceful gray-green foliage that turns silvery beneath and branches that become laden with bright orange berries by early September. It is one of the larger-growing named selections, forming a substantial multi-stemmed shrub or small tree over time, so give it room compared with more compact cultivars. As with all sea buckthorn it is dioecious and needs a male plant nearby to set fruit, and its nitrogen-fixing roots make it well suited to poor, sandy, or windswept sites. Because ripe berries cling tightly to the stem, most growers harvest by cutting whole fruiting branches to strip or freeze rather than picking by hand.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Red Candy is self-fertile and can bear a light summer crop followed by a heavier fall crop.

directions: Red Candy is a Dutch-bred patented lingonberry selection prized for its dense, compact, mounding habit and unusually heavy flower and fruit set relative to its small size, typically staying under a foot tall while spreading into a tidy evergreen mat. Loose clusters of nodding, pink-blushed white spring flowers give way to abundant bright scarlet berries that ripen earlier and more prolifically than many older lingonberry cultivars. It shares the acidic, humus-rich soil preferences of blueberries and makes an excellent edible groundcover beneath other ericaceous shrubs. Shear plantings back lightly every few years to renew vigor and maintain dense, productive growth.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: Howes was selected from the wild around 1843 by Eli Howes of East Dennis, Massachusetts, and became one of the foundational heirloom cultivars that built the New England cranberry industry, alongside Early Black and Searles. It ripens late in the season and produces small to medium, firm, deep-red berries with excellent keeping quality, historically prized for winter storage before modern refrigeration. Vines are moderately vigorous and well adapted to traditional bog culture with winter flooding and sanding. Because it ripens later than Early Black, Howes needs a fairly long, frost-free fall window to fully color, making it best suited to milder cranberry-growing regions.
sources: University of Massachusetts Amherst Cranberry Station

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: Searles was discovered as a wild seedling in 1893 near Wisconsin Rapids, Wisconsin, and went on to become one of the historically dominant heirloom cultivars of the North American cranberry industry, still accounting for a meaningful share of Wisconsin bog acreage today. It is a medium-early ripening selection producing large, bright red berries, though the fruit does not store as long as Howes and is generally used soon after harvest rather than kept for winter storage. Vines are vigorous and well suited to the cooler bog conditions of the upper Midwest, tolerating traditional winter flooding for cold protection. As with all cranberries, success depends on strongly acidic, saturated bog soil and a reliable irrigation or flood source.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: Crowley is a 1961 cross of McFarlin and Prolific developed as part of mid-twentieth-century efforts to breed cranberries better suited to processing rather than the fresh market. It produces medium-sized, dark red berries with good color development, making it valued for juice and sauce production rather than for fresh whole-berry sales. Vines show the vigor typical of McFarlin parentage while ripening somewhat more uniformly, and they respond well to the same bog culture, winter flooding, and sanding practices used for other cranberry cultivars. It remains a minor but historically notable selection in breeding programs tracing the development of modern processing cranberries.
sources: Frontiers in Plant Science — cranberry cultivar genotyping studies

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in a sheltered site with moist, acidic, well-drained soil; grow in a container and overwinter under cover in colder zones.

directions: Flambeau is a variegated sport of Chilean guava grown as much for its ornamental foliage as its fruit, with cream, green, and soft pink leaf coloring that stands out year-round in a border or container. It produces the same small, aromatic, red berries with a strawberry-vanilla flavor as the species, though typically in lighter quantity than green-leaved selections since variegated growth is somewhat less vigorous. It ripens earlier in the season than many Chilean guava plantings, extending the harvest window when grown alongside standard green forms. Give it a sheltered spot in partial shade to full sun and protect it from hard frost, since variegated foliage is generally less cold tolerant than the straight species.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in a sheltered site with lime-free, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Ka Pow is a vigorous Chilean guava selection popularized for bearing noticeably larger fruit than typical seedling plants, and for cropping while still young. Fragrant soft pink flowers appear over a long season and are followed by aromatic red berries with a flavor often compared to wild strawberries crossed with lily of the valley. It grows into a denser, more upright shrub than some older Chilean guava selections and tolerates light frost down to around 20°F once established, though a sheltered site is still recommended in marginal climates. Grow in lime-free, well-drained soil and use as a hedge, container specimen, or mixed-border shrub in mild coastal gardens.
